entries.title: 5 Best Smart Speakers (2026): Alexa, Google, Apple
entries.summary: Looking to add a smart speaker to your house? Here’s which to choose, whether you’re an Alexa, Siri, or Gemini fan.
entries.content:
There are three big players in the running for the best smart speaker: Amazon, Google, and Apple. Each voice-assistant-powered system has its own benefits and limitations, and you’ll have to consider several factors to pinpoint the right smart speaker for your needs.

You may already have a favorite ecosystem. Maybe it's the one that’s compatible with your phone, as an Apple or Android user. Or maybe it's Amazon's Alexa, if you already own one of the many speakers that the company launched following the 2014 arrival of the first Amazon Echo. Amazon's smart-speaker fleet, in particular, is expansive, often seeing multiple new models every year, while the offerings are much narrower for Google and Apple. That said, a few months ago, Google did launch a new smart speaker for the first time in years—the 2026 Google Home Speaker—and I share my thoughts on it in this guide.

After trying nearly every single smart speaker that's come out in the last decade, I have a sense of the best options available today to fit various needs. Also, check out my guides to the Best Alexa Speakers, Best Google Speakers, and Best Smart Displays if you want more insight into each category.

Updated September 2026: I've added details about Amazon’s increased prices and which speakers were affected, and noted that the Google Nest Hub Max is currently out of stock online.

The Best Smart Speakers

Best for Google Users

Google's latest smart speaker, the Google Home Speaker (8/10, WIRED Recommends), is an amalgamation of great features from other smart speakers. It shares its name with the original Google speaker from 2016, but its shape and size are reminiscent of an Apple HomePod Mini. It has the tap controls and fun colors I remember from the older Google Nest Mini. And it joins the rest of Google’s smart speakers (other than the Google Pixel Tablet with the charging dock) by using Google Gemini as the default assistant instead of Google Assistant.

Gemini does sound impressively human, offering answers that approximate an interaction with another person. Sometimes its answers get a little long-winded, so just be prepared for that. But Google Gemini is nonetheless a touch smarter than other assistants in its cohort; it’s able to answer questions about my own schedule and knows to check with me about my artist preference if a song I request has multiple covers.

Gemini for Home is free, but some features you might like to use are hidden behind paywalls. For instance, Google rebranded its video camera subscriptions to “Google Home Premium,” which bundles some smart-home assistant features and video storage into one price. There are two tiers: Standard ($10 per month or $100 per year), which includes 30 days of event-based video history, intelligent alerts for things like familiar faces and packages, Gemini Live, and an AI-based tool to help you create smart-home routines for your household. The Advanced tier ($20 per month or $200 per year) includes 60 days of event-based video history, 10 days of 24/7 video history, descriptive notifications, searchable video history, video event descriptions, and daily summaries of recorded events, plus everything in the cheaper plan.

Gemini Live is the main behind-the-paywall feature you might want; it lets you switch your smart speaker into a more conversational mode. Using this feature, I had a long, natural-feeling chat with my speaker that covered my 3-year-old’s sleep patterns, scalp sunburns, and the previous night’s Love Island episode. It worked well, but it's not a capability I imagine I’ll use when I'm not actively testing.

Gemini Live doesn't work on every Google speaker, but in addition to working on the Google Home Speaker, it also works on all three versions of its available smart displays, including two iterations of the Nest Hub. My favorite is the 10-inch Nest Hub Max; it doubles as a digital photo frame powered by Google Photos, which works much better than Amazon's clunky uploader and might even be a tool you're already using. Google accounts get up to 15 GB of free storage (that'll include any Gmail or Drive files, too), so there are a lot of photos you can store and display on this device.

The Nest Hub Max has a solid sound profile given its slim frame with two 10-watt tweeters and a 30-watt woofer. The 10-inch touchscreen is a great size for everything from controlling your smart home and streaming videos to pulling up recipes and enjoying your own photos. Many of these capabilities rely on the smart display, which means you couldn't access them with a screen-free smart speaker. It's not the only smart display option on the market, but it has a prettier interface than Amazon's Echo Show 11 (below), and unlike on the Show 11, you won't see any ads sliding onto the screen on this Nest. There's also a camera for video calls and gesture-based controls. While there’s no cover for the camera, you can disable it if you prefer.

However, the Nest Hub Max seems to be completely out of stock at all retailers. I'm hoping we see it return, or get news of a new version. But we'll have to wait and see.

Best for Amazon Users

Most of the smart speakers I spot in friends' homes come from the Amazon Echo line. Options abound, and many that I see are older models, like the puck-shaped Echo Dot. Such dated speakers are still fairly well-supported, though not all of them can gain access to Alexa+, Amazon's newer AI-powered voice assistant. But even if your smart speaker can use Alexa+, it's only worth the upgrade if you have Amazon Prime, which includes access to the assistant. Without a Prime subscription, you'd have to pay $20 a month for Alexa+ on its own. It's literally cheaper to get Amazon Prime ($15 a month for most plans), which comes with a wider range of benefits. This price model is surely intentional, as it may serve as a push to get you to sign up for Prime if you haven't already.

The Echo Dot Max is one of Amazon's newest models. It launched in late 2025, taking the small form from past Dot models and upgrading the device with impressive sound quality, a built-in smart-home hub, Alexa and Alexa+ access, and a slightly different look. It’s surprisingly loud without getting muddled, especially considering its small size. Impressively, it can still hear my requests even when the room is loud or it is playing loud music. I tested it against the latest Echo Studio last year and found the speakers were more similar in quality than I expected. The Dot Max is more expensive than older Dot models; if you don’t need next-level sound, the more affordable Echo Dot (fifth gen) might be a good fit for your needs.

Both the Echo Dot Max and the Echo Dot were hit by price increases at the end of August. Amazon raised prices across its product categories, including its Echo speakers. The Echo Dot Max got a $20 increase and a new $120 price tag, while the Echo Dot (5th Gen) went from $50 to $80. I'm most disappointed about the Echo Dot, since now its sale prices will likely only go down to the $50 range instead of landing between $25 and $30. It makes it a less appealing buy at its new price, and I recommend waiting for a sale for both of these models.

If you're looking for something with more capabilities, like being able to read recipes, stream shows, and even make video calls, you might want a smart display instead of a smart speaker. These devices can perform the same functions as any other smart speaker, but they add a screen and camera to unlock a variety of new abilities.

Amazon launched two new smart displays last fall: The Echo Show 11 ($250) is the pricier of the two, but I liked it better than the new Echo Show 8 ($200). The Show 11 has better sound, and its 11-inch screen was a nice size for both my desk and kitchen counter. The interface is updated for Alexa+, but I didn’t love some of the changes. For instance, when you ask Alexa+ questions, the Show 11 brings up a chat-like interface. Because of this, some answers don’t provide the same level of detail as I got with the original Alexa. The change that I like the least is how Alexa+ handles the weather; I loved seeing the pages of weather info for the day and week that original Alexa would show, and now I just get a small snippet in a sea of written words. If you want something similar but cheaper, I'd recommend the older third-generation Echo Show 8 ($150) over the newest one. That model had a better sound when I tested both Echo Show 8 versions side by side.

It's also important to note that Echo Show devices have a lot of screen clutter, and the devices also show ads. You might not see the ads right away, but eventually you'll start seeing prompts to buy things on Amazon. You can activate photo mode to hide the ads, but that will only last three hours before going back to regular mode. You can also remove clutter (like the multiple news, sports, and food-related topics it'll show by default) by going into the device's settings. An Echo Show device can technically double as a digital photo frame, but it's annoying to upload pictures and won't put vertical photos side-by-side.

Neither the Echo Show 11 nor the older Echo Show 8 increased in price like the Echo Dot Max, but the newer Echo Show 8 did and is now retailing for a base price of $200. It's on sale right now to match the price of the older model, though, so that's a pro for now. The new prices really just make my two preferred options an even better buy than before—just a $20 increase to get the Echo Show 11 over the new Show 8 is well worth the better sound and larger screen.

Best for Apple Users

Smart speaker options are the most limited for Apple users. My colleagues and I weren’t impressed by the sound quality of the larger HomePod when it relaunched in 2023. But the smaller HomePod Mini is a fine investment for the price, and you'll find it to be the most convenient option if you already use the Apple Home app and Siri.

It's about a third of the price and smaller than the full-size speaker; otherwise, it’s capable of just about everything the larger model can do. It doubles as a smart home hub to connect your Apple-compatible devices, so you don't need the larger speaker or Apple TV if you're mainly looking for smart-home control. It's still not my favorite smart speaker overall, and Apple HomeKit isn't my favorite ecosystem. It has serious limitations, and I find myself running into more issues adding my devices to the Home app than on any other platform. But if you're committed to your Apple ecosystem, this is the speaker to buy.

There's also no smart display option in Apple's ecosystem, so if you'd like one of those in your home, you'll have to go with Google or Apple. Notably, Apple's price hikes in June affected both the Apple HomePod Mini and the larger HomePod. The HomePod Mini used to be $99 but now retails for $129.

Comparing Our Favorite Smart Speakers

Capable of lossless high definition. Has a built-in smart-home hub and tap controls Limited one-year warranty, extended warranty available for purchase; 30-day returns

Honorable Mentions

There are tons of smart speakers available for purchase. Here are a few more that I like:

Amazon's Echo Spot for $110 is a great partial smart display. While the music quality doesn't offer the same depth you'll get on the Echo Dot, the fun little half-screen display on this second-gen Echo Spot proves useful. It shows time, weather, your calendar, and the name of the song playing. It's a nice set of features that make it a great speaker for the bedroom, especially since its lack of a camera removes any visual privacy concerns. It used to be $80, but was affected by Amazon's price increases and now has a starting price of $110.

Amazon’s Echo Show 8 (third gen) for $150 is the best Alexa smart display for the money. It's smaller than my top-pick Echo Show 11, but if you're OK with the size, know that the sound here is better than what you’ll get on the newer Echo Show 8. Though older, this edition is still enabled for Alexa+ and has a built-in smart-home hub. It's also one of the few Amazon Echo Show models that wasn't hit by Amazon's price hikes.

Amazon’s Echo Studio (second gen) for $220 is the best-sounding Alexa speaker. I love this smart speaker for its fantastic sound quality and power, built-in smart-home hub, and spatial audio capabilities. While it's smaller than the Apple HomePod, it easily filled my entire second-floor great room with music. It also escaped the price hikes and maintains the same price tag that it had at launch.

Why Did Amazon Echo Prices Increase?

Amazon raised prices for several of its products in August, including many Echo speaker models. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED, but a spokesperson told CNET it was due to rising costs for memory and storage components. However, many affordable models were affected rather than higher-tier models. It's unclear if this is due to those powerful models already being priced appropriately, or if Amazon is looking to pass off mediocre sales prices as better deals with deal events like the fall Prime Day and Black Friday around the corner.

Here are all the Echo models affected:

  • Echo Dot (5th Gen): $80 (up $30)
  • Echo Spot (2nd Gen): $110 (up $30)
  • Echo Dot Max: $120 (up $20)
  • Echo Show 5 (3rd Gen): $100 (up $10)
  • Echo Show 8 (4th Gen): $200 (up $20)
  • Echo Show 11: $250 (up $30)
  • Echo Show 15: $350 (up $50)
  • Echo Show 21: $500 (up $100)

What’s Alexa+?

Amazon announced the new and improved Alexa, named Alexa+, in February 2025. This second generation of the Alexa voice assistant is more conversational than its predecessor, offering an experience similar to what you get with AI assistants like ChatGPT. This makes sense, given that Alexa+ was built on generative AI. Alexa+ does a better job at answering a variety of questions than first-gen Alexa and responds quickly to all kinds of requests. You can learn about my firsthand experience with Alexa+ here.

Alexa+ is free for Amazon Prime members. If you aren’t a member, you can get a free trial of the new assistant for 30 days, but after that, a subscription carries a $20 monthly fee. At that point, it’s cheaper to join Prime than it is to subscribe to Alexa+. This is likely by design to hook you into Amazon's larger ecosystem. Yes, the Prime subscription fee is a big jump from being free, but most people who choose to get an Amazon Alexa device in the first place are also likely Prime subscribers. If you aren't, though, this assistant isn't worth the cost of the subscription.

Alexa+ also requires that all voice recordings be sent to Amazon for processing, and Amazon has changed its policy for recordings with regular Alexa, too—those now also go to Amazon. There was previously a “Do Not Send Voice Recordings” privacy feature that you could select, which would process voice requests locally, but Amazon killed that functionality last year. The privacy change will affect all users, whether or not you sign up for Alexa+, regardless of whether you're using an Alexa+-compatible device or not.

What’s Gemini for Google Home?

Google announced late last year that Gemini for Home, the new version of its voice assistant, is rolling out to existing Google Home users. It's replaced the previous Google Assistant entirely and is currently slated to roll out to almost all of Google's devices. One of the notable exceptions is the Pixel Tablet; otherwise, Google's existing hardware properly reflects what Gemini for Home will reach.

Unlike Alexa+, this new assistant will always be free. However, Google is changing its camera subscription, Nest Aware, to become a new subscription named Google Home Premium. As I mentioned above in my pick for the best smart speaker for Google users, this subscription has two tiers, Standard ($10 a month) and Advanced ($20 a month). Beyond cameras, each option includes several advanced smart assistant features.

Also Tested

Amazon's Echo Hub for $180: The Echo Hub is designed to control your smart devices entirely. It acts more like a home security device than a true smart speaker. However, it also has the worst built-in speaker of Alexa's ecosystem, since it's designed to be used in tandem with a more powerful Alexa speaker, like the ones above.

Amazon Echo Pop for $40: The Echo Pop is a cute little speaker that's affordable and comes in fun colors. It's a fine choice for college students or teenagers who want something with a little personality, but everyone else should just upgrade to the Echo Dot for much better sound and the same features otherwise. It fluctuates a lot whether it's in stock, and often doesn't pop up when I search Amazon's site, but it's currently still available.

Amazon Echo Show 5 (3rd Gen) for $100: The Show 5 has the same capabilities as the Show 8, but on a smaller, less convenient screen. It's a good size for a bedroom, but it has a camera, which many don't want in that space. I'd rather add the Echo Spot or the Google Nest Hub for a similar mini screen—hold the camera—on my bedside table. It did go up $10 when Amazon raised its product prices in August.

Amazon Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) for $200: This is a solid smart speaker with Amazon's latest physical design and Alexa+ right out of the box. But it's not a sound improvement over the older model, so I'd personally pick the third-gen option (see above) or upgrade to the Echo Show 11 ($250), especially since it's only a $50 difference after the fourth-gen Show 8 went up in price with other Echo speakers and Amazon devices.

Amazon Echo Show 15 for $350: The Show 15 exists somewhere on the continuum of being a smart display and a smart TV, but it doesn't quite fully nail being either. The widgets are fun to use since you can add so many to the Show's 15-inch screen. But after trying this device a few times, it’s left me underwhelmed. The Show 15 grew on me while I was using it with Alexa+, though, particularly with a stand ($125) to sit on my desk. But it's still larger than I need for day-to-day tasks, and smaller than what I'd want from a television, and it increased $50 during Amazon's August price hikes.

Apple HomePod for $349: Apple's flagship smart speaker has a muddy midrange and high-end, which is disappointing for the price point. The HomePod does have a lot of bass, though, if that's your jam. If you want an Apple-powered smart speaker in your home, the Mini is nearly a third of the price and has capabilities nearly identical to the full-size model. The price also increased from $299 to $349 last month after Apple increased all of its prices.

Google Nest Audio for $95: This is still a good smart speaker that has Google Gemini for Home and Gemini Live compatibility, but unless you buy it on a serious sale, there's no reason not to buy the newest model instead to make sure you don't miss out on features in the future. It's becoming harder and harder to find in stock, so if your heart is set on one, don't wait.

Google Nest Hub for $100: This petite smart display is a great bedside speaker for Google users. The 7-inch screen feels like a smartphone propped up on its side rather than a massive smart display. It also has motion-sense technology built in to track your sleep, which is a handy feature for people who don't find sleep-tracking wearables comfortable. Plus, no camera. But it's rapidly going out of stock at third-party retailers, and likely won't be available for much longer.

JBL Authentics 200 for $380: This was my previous pick for a third-party smart speaker, but I'm uncertain of its ability to access Amazon’s and Google's newest assistants. I'll retest it once I confirm if it will gain access to one (if not both) assistants.

Sonos Era 100 for $219: Another third-party option, but it won't grant access to Google support. You can connect it to Amazon Alexa, though. Sonos is a great investment if you're really looking for a great speaker that can have smarts—but its smart assistant isn't the primary feature.

Sonos Beam Gen 2 for $499: This is an older version of the Sonos Beam that still has Google support, but I'm uncertain if it'll gain access to Gemini for Home.

WiiM A10 for $229: This speaker doesn't have a voice assistant, but it does have compatibility with AirPlay 2, Google Cast, and Siri to be used as a Bluetooth speaker. WIRED reviewer Parker Hall says it reminds him of a Sonos speaker, but that it can instantly connect with Spotify Connect—faster than any other speaker he's tried.

FAQs

How Should You Choose Between Alexa, Google, and Siri?

The easiest way to choose which smart assistant to add to your house is to consider which ecosystem you're already using in some capacity. If you're a big Google or Android user, for example, adding a Google Gemini–powered speaker to your home is a no-brainer. It's not always that simple, though. If you’re an Apple and iPhone user, you’ll find benefits in choosing HomeKit-powered devices. But because Apple's ecosystem is so limited, you might want to choose a different assistant for the devices you want. Amazon's Alexa has the widest range of offerings, but Google's seamless experience has me coming back again and again.

Here's what you should ask yourself to decide:

  • What assistant are you already using, if any?
  • What products do you want to use in your home, and which assistants are they compatible with?
  • What features do you want in a smart speaker? Which ecosystem can offer you those features?

Why Do I Prefer Google Devices?

There are many reasons to love Amazon’s Alexa voice assistant, and it works pretty well. If you want to use your voice assistant to shop or use Amazon services like Prime Music or Prime Video, chances are an Alexa-powered speaker is best for you.

Google's smart speakers have fewer skills and are compatible with fewer smart-home devices than Alexa, but Google Gemini, like Google Assistant before it, can do enough to qualify as truly useful—plus, Google adds new skills fairly frequently. Speakers with Google Gemini continue to work better when you network them together, and they're compatible with a wide variety of Google apps and services. Google is better at answering random questions and telling you where to go out to eat, since it can access and send information to your phone through Google apps.

Spotify, Pandora, and YouTube Music are the main ways to play music with Google Gemini. The service can also send Netflix shows and movies to your TV if you have a Chromecast attached.

If you're using a smart display, I also prefer Google’s options to Amazon's, mainly because Alexa Show devices serve you sponsored content while Google's will not. Amazon's Show displays are already crowded with content by default that you'll likely want to remove. (To do so, go to Settings on the device, and then click Home Content. You'll currently find more than 40 options you can toggle on and off.) But you can't fully remove the sponsored content unless you're in Photo Frame mode. Meanwhile, Google's displays make for better photo frames, thanks to Google Photos. These displays also have a less crowded interface, with less content to distract you. I'd stick to a Nest Home Hub unless you definitely want an Alexa display and won't mind the occasional onscreen ad.

How Can I Get the Most Out of My Smart Speaker?

My biggest piece of advice for enjoying a smart speaker to its fullest potential is to make sure you put it somewhere you'll use it often. I love having a small speaker in my bedroom to ask about the weather while I'm getting ready for the day, and then I make sure there's a smart speaker somewhere near my desk and living area (usually multiple, but I'm an odd case since I test these for a living) so that I can call out requests as I work, cook, and watch TV.

The next biggest to-do for maximizing your smart speaker is to invest in other compatible smart-home gadgets. Smart speakers work best when they have other devices to control and speak to. Set up some smart lights, a smart lock or two, a video doorbell, a couple of security cameras—you name it! And then command your smart speaker to help you control them or otherwise check on your home.

Can I Use My Smart Speaker With My TV or Entertainment System?

Sometimes! This varies by TV model and what’s connected to your TV. You can find some TVs that have built-in voice control, though some might use voice control through the remote rather than with the smart speaker. Apple's smart speakers and Apple TV sync the best among single-system options I've tested. But otherwise, I haven't found it as painless as I would have hoped.

If you're looking for music entertainment, smart speakers are great. You can connect multiple smart speakers for a stereo system, or connect your smart speaker to existing systems. Depending on the system in question and what you already have, you might have to choose a smart speaker with a 3.5-mm wire-in option or a speaker that has built-in compatibility with Amazon Alexa and Google Gemini for Home.

Should I Be Concerned About My Privacy?

Adding microphones to your home (and sometimes cameras) is a valid point of concern. Smart speakers are technically always listening, though they're supposed to only listen for their wake word and otherwise ignore all other audio until asked a question. But there have been cases where police have requested audio recordings from smart speakers to use as evidence, including two separate murder cases in 2018 and 2019.

Most of the speakers I recommend have some method to shut down the speaker's listening tendencies, whether an off switch or a camera cover, but it's annoying to switch on and off if you want to use your speaker regularly. Alexa also no longer allows local processing, so everything you ask Alexa is now sent to the cloud to help Alexa+ run.

Ultimately, you should be concerned about your privacy, and it's worth considering whether you want a set of microphones in your house. In my years of testing, I haven't felt any of my smart speakers to be invasive, and they do a good job giving themselves away when activated (lighting up and asking “Hmm?” if they don't understand the question), so it's never felt like my speakers are sneakily listening to me. But it's certainly a personal choice.

Will Smart Speakers Become Bricks?

The smart speakers in this guide are primarily made by large brands—Amazon! Google! Sonos!—and it's unlikely any of them will suddenly vanish or become a useless brick speaker on your desk. There are even some first-generation Amazon Echos still working that are about a decade old (with mixed results, based on what users say online).

But a UK law passed in April 2024 adds more protection here. The law mandates three key points: more secure password procedures, more clarity on how to report bugs and security issues, and that manufacturers and retailers must inform customers how long these products will receive support and software updates.

The last point is the most relevant for smart speaker users, since the fear is that you'll buy a speaker that will suddenly stop getting updates and become unusable. I'll be watching to see how much information is really offered to shoppers as it takes effect, but so far, we haven't seen any changes. Nonetheless, it's a law we like. While there's not yet an equivalent law in the US, I'll watch for updates here as well.

How Does WIRED Test Smart Speakers?

I employ a variety of tests with smart speakers. I do microphone tests, gauging how far away a speaker will hear and respond to a question, both while music is playing and while music is off. I also play a variety of songs to see how well the speaker performs at playing everything from chill lo-fi to my favorite metal band and beyond. I also sync it with smart devices to see how well it connects and controls those devices, and what kind of capabilities it has. If there's a screen, I also test the included features. Finally, I also live with these speakers for at least a week (if not more like months!) to see how they fare in day-to-day use and long-term performance.

How Does WIRED Acquire Smart Speakers? What Does WIRED Do With Them After Testing Them?

Most of the smart speakers I test are press samples that brands send to me. I obtain these samples with the understanding that no coverage is promised, nor are there any agreements about what that possible coverage will look like. I also occasionally purchase my own speakers.

After testing, I keep most smart speakers for long-term testing or in storage for future comparison tests. If I deem a smart speaker redundant, I usually recycle the device locally, as it likely won't receive more updates or support from the company. If it's still a viable speaker, I'll donate it instead.

entries.title: Insta360 X6 Review (2026): A Great 360 and Action Camera Hybrid
entries.summary: Insta360’s latest 360-degree camera uses larger sensors for better low-light performance and has a smaller body.
entries.content:
Larger sensors provide clearer, sharper video. Low-light performance improvements. 8K/50 fps 360 video. Shoot both 4K linear files and 8K 360 video simultaneously. Smaller body. Built-in storage and microSD card slot.

TIRED

Unresponsive haptic buttons. Mediocre pro recording features.

The combination of good video quality and user-friendly software has kept Insta360 at the forefront of the 360 camera world even as competitors like DJI and GoPro have carved out their own niche. With its latest camera, the Insta360 X6, the company is hoping to leap ahead of the pack again.

The Insta360 X6 brings a slightly larger sensor, faster video frame rates, better low-light performance, and tools to help you spend less time editing and more time filming. While it’s not a huge leap over its predecessor, the X6 is a solid improvement with several new features that might make upgrading worth it for some users.

What’s New

The X6 looks a little bit like if the X5 and the GoPro Max 2 had a baby. It’s shorter, squatter, and a tad bit wider than the X5, but not as small as the Max 2. That might sound like I’m setting it up to say it’s the Goldilocks size, but that’s not really the case. I actually like the individual sizes of the X5 and Max 2 better, the first for its narrower profile and the second for its much smaller overall size.

Along with the smaller size come two other major changes from the X5: the screen is smaller, and the physical buttons at the bottom are gone. Though there is noticeably less coverage, I didn’t find the smaller screen to make much difference. I could still see what I wanted to shoot, but the point of a 360 camera is you don’t need to frame shots. The main thing I use the screen for is making sure that the stitch line isn’t on my main subject.

I do miss the X5’s physical buttons on the front, one to record and the other for the menu. There is still a record button, now on the side of the X6, but the onscreen buttons just aren’t as good. They provide haptic feedback (the buttons vibrate when you press them), but they don’t respond 100 percent of the time. I found them noticeably harder to activate compared to the X5’s physical buttons, and I prefer the X5’s front button to start recording.

Another change to the outside is one of the better things about the X6: There are now power contact points on the bottom, which means you can attach a powered selfie stick and charge your camera while you use it. This is a great new feature that I hope other manufacturers copy. And don’t worry, the standard 1/4-inch tripod mount is still there.

Insta360 also says the X6’s new replaceable lens covers are harder than those on previous models. I have never scratched the lenses on my X5, nor did I acquire any scratches during the couple of months I tested the X6. The camera has an IP68 rating, and it’s dustproof and waterproof down to 66 feet.

Speaking of batteries, perhaps my favorite thing about the redesigned X6 is that the battery is now … just a battery. In older X-series cameras, the battery door was part of the battery, which always seemed unnecessary and meant there was no chance of ever using the same battery in another Insta360 camera, like the Ace Pro 2. Now that is potentially possible. If you’re listening, Insta360, give us the same battery for the Ace Pro 3 that’s in the X6. Battery size has also increased from 2,400 mAh to 2,600 mAh compared to the X5.

New Innards

The X6 uses a larger 1/1.1-inch sensor, the same size as the one in the DJI Osmo 360. That’s up from the 1/1.28-inch sensor in the X5 (and note that 360 cameras have two sensors since they have two lenses), and it gives you marginally sharper, clearer video. I did not notice a huge difference when recording in 360 mode. Of the Insta360, GoPro, and DJI cameras I’ve tested, I still find the GoPro Max 2 footage to be the best quality overall, and to GoPro’s point when it launched the Max 2, the X6 only records 7.2K video versus the Max 2’s 8K video.

At night, though, the X6 wins. It’s much brighter than the X5 or the GoPro for starters, and while sometimes it does render colors a little wonky, with blues tending toward green and yellows going more orange than they are in real life, it still produces the best 360-degree low-light footage I’ve shot. The Osmo 360 is a close second, but at times I find it has quite a bit of weird blur-like artifacts in low light.

One of the more exciting new features is single-lens mode, which, at least on the spec sheet, goes a long way to making the X6 a viable action camera replacement. I dream of one camera that can do it all, and the X6 is definitely closer than other 360 cameras in fulfilling that wish.

The X6 can now record up to 5K video in single-lens mode (up from 4K in the X5), but even better is the new InstaFrame 2.0 feature, which is Insta360’s name for the ability to record both 360 video and a single-lens shot at the same time. This greatly simplifies editing since you have a flat file to work from, and if you miss the shot in that one, you have the 360 footage to fall back on. This was always a great feature, but in the X5 the non-360 file was capped at 1080p, which made it less than useful. The X6 bumps that footage to 4K for the single-lens recording and up to 8K at 30 frames per second for the 360 footage recorded simultaneously, which makes this very usable and is, in fact, how I shot most of the time.

As I have said many times, no one wants to see raw 360 footage (yeah, yeah, I know VR is going to catch on one day, but I am not holding my breath), and while InstaFrame makes editing it down to a traditional linear video file about as easy as is possible, it is still kind of a pain. Advanced users will also find it annoying that you cannot use Insta360’s I-Log format (video log modes are to video what a RAW file is to still images, and capture a much wider dynamic range) with InstaFrame 2.0, but there are some pretty good preset color modes, and I recommend using them for everyday shots.

With I-Log, the X6 supports 10-bit recording when recording in 360 mode. In single-lens mode, you can only shoot in 8-bit I-Log. The higher the bit rate, the more color information is available (1,024 shades in 10-bit versus 256 in 8-bit). That’s a shame because, at least for my needs, this stops the X6 from replacing an action camera in my kit. Perhaps we’ll get this in the X7. For non-pro users, this is likely a moot point.

Other new features in the X6 include 47 GB of internal storage. There’s still a microSD card slot, which is what I used in almost all my testing, but it’s nice to have the internal storage for those times that you forget an SD card, as I do from time to time. Even though I don’t use the internal storage, I love that it’s there as a backup.

The photo tools also got a bump, with 120-megapixel images (up from 72 MP in the X5) and a new AI reframing feature. In this mode, just press the shutter button and the camera will take three photos, one facing you, one facing out at (presumably) your subject, and one of those tiny world images. (I find the first two photo styles useful, but the latter is lame.) You also get the original 360 photo.

To my mind, useful software-driven features, like the triple-photo feature and InstaFrame 2.0, are what have always separated Insta360 from GoPro and DJI. They make it easier to get usable images and video out of the camera.

Finally, I’d like to point out something I haven’t seen mentioned much, but I love how fast the X6 starts up. You press power, and it’s up and running in about 200 milliseconds, which is the fastest start-up time of any action or 360 camera I’ve tested.

360 for Newbies

If you already own the X5, this is very much an incremental update. The new features are nice to have, but the basic video quality is comparable to the X5. If you’ve been thinking of getting a 360 camera but haven’t pulled the trigger yet, the X6 is worth considering. While I prefer the GoPro Max 2 in many shooting scenarios, the X6 wins in low light. I also love the ability to use it as a 5K action camera when you don’t need the 360 footage, as well as the option to shoot 4K and 360 video at the same time, neither of which is possible with the GoPro Max 2. Throw in the very nice editing software Insta360 offers, and you’ve got a great option for 360 camera newcomers.

Scott Gilbertson is Operations Manager for the WIRED Reviews Team. He was previously a writer and editor for WIRED’s Webmonkey.com, covering the independent web and early internet culture. You can reach him at luxagraf.net. ... Read More

entries.title: Gen AI Tools Are Now Being Used to Push ‘Slop Jihad’
entries.summary: A new generation of Islamic terror supporters are using AI to spread ‘Slop Jihad’ to new audiences on TikTok.
entries.content:
Over a decade ago, the Islamic State released a disturbing video that depicted its members lowering men locked in a cage into a swimming pool and drowning them. Today, that video has been reproduced as a SpongeBob SquarePants cartoon depicting fish in orange jumpsuits inside the cage, as SpongeBob lowers the cage into the water while Squidward films the scene.

The video, shared on TikTok, is part of what a new report from the Institute of Strategic Dialogue (ISD) calls “Slop Jihad,” a trend where young supporters of Islamic terror groups like ISIS and al-Qaida appear to use generative AI tools to create fan edits, cartoons, and memes designed radicalize a new generation of online backing.

This shift “signals a fundamental transformation in the aesthetics of jihadist propaganda online,” concludes the report, which was shared exclusively with WIRED.

“The principal concern is the growing volume and diversity of material,” says Adam Hadley, executive director of Tech Against Terrorism, a UN-backed counter terrorism organization that has also written a report about the Slop Jihad trend. “Highly stylized AI-generated content can make violent Islamist extremist material more accessible to younger audiences while reducing the visibility of conventional terrorist branding. Users may encounter perpetrator glorification inadvertently through fan edits, cartoons, memes, and other entertainment-oriented formats, after which engagement can drive algorithmic recommendations of related, more overt propaganda.”

Islamic terror groups have long demonstrated their capacity to adapt to new media environments to get their messages to a wide audience online, leveraging new and emerging technologies to aid recruitment and create a decentralized network of propaganda. This was seen in the early 2020s Alt Jihad movement, which sought to co-opt the aesthetics of the alt-right in the Islamic terrorism content.

These groups have also been making use of generative AI technology for a number of years. In 2024, the Islamic State-affiliated news program News Harvest began using AI-generated anchors to help disseminate propaganda videos quickly and cheaply.

But today, the look and feel of the content produced with generative AI is markedly different.

“This is new and it's still growing, it has not peaked by any means,” says Moustafa Ayad, the research chair in global Islamism and counter terrorism at ISD. “There's always been really shoddy content that's been produced in the support ecosystem, but it wasn't SpongeBob SquarePants as the Islamic State.”

Generative AI tools have also been utilized to quickly and cheaply turn official content from terror groups into animated videos. In one example, one TikTok account was turning the weekly al-Naba newsletter from ISIS into anime.

The Slop Jihad trend has seen some pushback from more traditional supporters who don’t like the new aesthetic. “There seems to be some animosity towards it, because they don't believe the producers of Slop Jihad are true believers,” Ayad says, referring to some reactions to the SpongeBob video. “But again, some accounts that have shared traditional official propaganda are sharing the newer videos. So there seems to be a love-hate relationship with the Slop Jihad content.”

For years now, TikTok has been central to Islamic terror groups online messaging campaign, taking advantage of the platform’s powerful algorithmic recommendations to spread their message. A report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in 2024 found that TikTok was among the top 10 platforms used to spread terrorist and extremist content.

While Ayad did find a limited number of Slop Jihad videos on other platforms like Instagram and Facebook, the vast majority of the videos were found on TikTok. In total, he found 150 Slop Jihad videos from 71 accounts with more than 5.4 million total views on the platform. Ayad believes the prevalence of this content on TikTok is down to the platform’s For You Page algorithm “that is hyper-targeted to user interests.” He also credits the high level of general AI slop on the platform and “an existing entrenched ecosystem of jihadist support on the platform.”

TikTok contested the findings of the report. "This report's vague methodology reaches poorly evidenced conclusions and doesn't reflect how people use our platform,” a TikTok spokesperson tells WIRED. “We prohibit the presence of violent and hateful organisations, and we use a combination of advanced moderation technology, safety teams, and partnerships to proactively detect and remove violative content, as we keep TikTok a safe space for our community. All the content referenced in this report has been removed from TikTok."

Dozens of the videos identified by ISD for their report were deleted after WIRED shared them with TikTok.

WIRED shared the ISD report with several outside experts on Islamic terror groups' use of social media to radicalize followers, and all broadly agreed with ISD’s findings. “What is notable here is the ease with which generative AI allows a much broader and more decentralized set of users to remix jihadi figures and imagery and the extent to which that material can circulate across communities whose interest may be driven as much by violence, trolling, or notoriety as by actual commitment to jihadi ideology,” Aaron Zelin, a researcher who specializes in Jihadi extremism at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, tells WIRED.

While Ayad admits that some of the wilder Slop Jihad content may be difficult to identify as terror-related, much of it is very clearly supportive of terror groups and ideologies. TikTok has taken down some of the accounts Ayad was monitoring, but many of them have backup accounts in place and have signaled to their followers where they can find them in the case of a takedown.

“Some of the content is surviving for months at a time and continues to evade moderation efforts, whether it's their AI system that's meant to detect terrorist material or not,” Ayad says.

entries.title: Le Creuset x Star Trek Collection: Prices, availability, release date
entries.summary: Vulcan oven mitts, spaceship baking dishes, and an out-of-this-world communicator grater—you'll need warp speed to Klingon to this limited edition kitchen kit, ideal for perfecting the broth of Khan.
entries.content:
Logic clearly dictates that the needs of the penne outweigh the needs of the stew, or the bun. While this would have been a gloriously fan-faithful reason for Le Creuset, the French-Belgian maker of colorful cookware for more than a century, to materialize its new limited-edition Star Trek collection, the range is being launched in celebration of 60 years of the cult sci-fi show.

No matter, because when you have such stellar items as Vulcan oven mitts, shuttlecraft baking dishes, and—perhaps best of all—a cheese grater in the shape of the classic Trek communicator (which has somewhat wonderfully been nicknamed the “Communi-grator” by Le Creuset's design team), there's only cause for celebration in the cosmos.

Going on sale today, to coincide with the space series' 60th anniversary, the limited-edition collection has actually been in development for years after Le Creuset approached Paramount to collaborate on the kitchen kit in time for the landmark birthday. Le Creuset is no stranger to fun mashups, with its recent 2024 Pokemon collection being snapped up almost instantly (those looking to get pieces now have to scour the likes of eBay for items way over original retail prices).

As well as the 15 cm Communi-grator for $68 (£52), foodies looking for Federation-themed gear might appreciate the $500 (£425) Enterprise round casserole pot complete with Starfleet insignia knob, or the $450 (£385) Klingon shallow casserole dish with trefoil "Heart of Virtue" knob—both in cast iron. Inside the Enterprise NCC-1701 pot is the legend “to boldly go”, while the Klingon dish offers up an encouraging “Qapla!” (“success” in Klingon), handy for experimental cooking.

Carrying culinary adventures into the unknown comes the Le Creuset x Star Trek: Galileo shuttlecraft casserole dish ($150), which has a roomy 1.6 liters of space inside. Vulcan votaries are well catered for with the $35 (£31) Spock ear mug (perfect for Vulcan spice tea), complete with gold detailing along the rim as a nod to the Starfleet uniform; the $55 (£36) Spock hand spoon rest; and the whimsical Vulcan salute “live long and prosper” oven mitt, resplendent in signature Star Trek baby blue for $40 (£36).

Not merely content with digitally launching the collection online, Le Creuset engaged Sent Into Space to boldly send its Enterprise casserole dish where no pan has gone before—more than 111,000 feet above the Earth, atop 99.5 percent of the planet’s atmosphere. While obviously a blatant (albeit fitting) marketing stunt, there's actually some considerable logistics to overcome in sending a cast-iron pot to the edge of space.

Sent Into Space co-founder Chris Rose had the task of launching the pot in the stratosphere via a space-capable balloon taller than the height of The White House, where it stayed for 1 hour, 19 minutes, and 4 seconds enduring temperatures down to -63.4°C (-82.12°F). “Because of the weight, we had to give some serious consideration to how we were going to hold things, making sure everything was very balanced,” Rose tells WIRED. Rose and his team also have to rely on simulations to take into account considerations such as where will the pot land as it's parachuted back down to Earth, as well as how to avoid bodies of water and built-up areas, for example.

“The legal authorities within the aviation community need to know. We can't have a Le Creuset casserole dish floating past the window of an airborne A380 as it makes its way off to some destination,” Rose says. “So we are in constant communication, both from a flight-clearance perspective before this ever leaves leaves the ground, to onboard systems for telemetry and communication.” Indeed, in the early stages of reentry, Rose says the Enterprise casserole dish reached speeds in excess of 300 mph before slowing and landing safely in Lincolnshire, England.

Back on terra firma, the Le Creuset x Star Trek collection should serve cadets and captains alike, provided you can secure your selections before stock vanishes like a cloaked Bird-of-Prey.

entries.title: Home Depot Labor Day Sale (2026): BOGO on Best Grills and Tools
entries.summary: The Home Depot Labor Day sale goes hard on grills and tools. Here are our recommendations on what to buy—and what to ignore.
entries.content:
Labor Day sales are the last gasp of summer DIY season, and it almost always means steep discounts on tools and batteries—especially as retailers clear inventory space for the holidays. The Home Depot Labor Day sale goes pretty hard this year, bolstering the usual battery of BOGO deals, as well as end-of-season grill discounts.

Alas, not everything is a winner. The smart home and home-security deals I've seen for Home Depot are either not great deals—or they're on older models or services like Ring that WIRED doesn't recommend for privacy reasons. Check out WIRED's Best Tech Labor Day Deals of 2026, or the Best Amazon Labor Day Deals, if this is what you're after.

But here are the best deals on tools and grills that I've found for 2026's Home Depot Labor Day sale, or check out my colleague Kat Merck's Labor Day deals guide to getting an excellent tool starter kit for less than $400. You can also browse Home Depot's Labor Day deals by category, but fair warning: There's a lot to sift through.

Home Depot Labor Day Grill and Griddle Deals

The steepest Labor Day price cuts are often on grills and griddles. At Home Depot, the best deals are on Traeger's stock of pellet smokers that offer easy temperature control, but maybe a little less smoke than charcoal or wood cookers. These have the side benefit of maintaining utility through the cool months. In the temperate, four-season Pacific Northwest, I actually far prefer fall to summer as a grill and smoker season.

Discounts include a cool hundo off the basic model of Traeger's Woodridge smart pellet grill, whose bigger, upgraded version, the Woodridge Pro (8/10, WIRED Recommends), was WIRED's previous top-pick pellet smoker. Its no-fuss operation and cleaning, sophisticated temperature control, and absolute beastly capacity set it apart. But Home Depot's steepest discount is on Traeger's standby, entry-level Pro 22 smoker. We have not tested this recently, but after a dozen years it's a near-classic, and $390 is the lowest price it's seen all year.

Other deals among WIRED-recommended grills include $50 off a couple of Weber's durable, last-you-forever standbys—the Weber Kettle and the Weber Spirit E-210. I and fellow WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson tend to love these two models precisely because they are basic, durable, reliable, and low-cost. The Weber Kettle, especially, can be upgraded with smart features into a temp-controlled, smart-charcoal beast.

This $50 off deal tends to be the standard Weber deal. But the price already starts out affordable, and so the sale price amounts to an excellent value on a grill that's likely to be with you a while. If you'd like your kettle in green, you can get it for half off, a mere $100.

Home Depot Milwaukee Tool Deals

Buying power tools is all about picking an ecosystem (and a battery pack). WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson favors Milwaukee for its intersection between reliability and value, and for tentpole sales Home Depot usually offers free battery packs or buy-one-get one deals.

One of the best and most versatile tools Gilbertson recommends is Milwaukee's excellent impact driver ($179). Lucky you: During the Labor Day sale, this comes free with the purchase of the portable M18 battery you'll need to operate it wirelessly. If you've already got a Milwaukee battery, the BOGO still holds for an assortment of tools including an oscillating multi-tool that's also one of the more underrated tools in the DIYer home kit.

Home Depot Ryobi Landscaping and Tool Deals

Ryobi is the brand that former WIRED reviewer Parker Hall has consistently recommended for yard and landscaping tools, in large part because of their service philosophy. In many regions including mine (the Pacific Northwest), Ryobi keeps a local repair technician on retainer to come and fix your mower or blower, instead of making you ship your machine to a repair center somewhere. This is clutch, even if you won't have to use the service often.

Home Depot is offering its usual BOGO battery deals on Ryobi's landscaping tools, including the heavy-duty leaf blower ($159) you're going to need sooner than you expect.

For entry-level tool kits, my colleague Kat Merck also recommends this shockingly low-cost starter power tool kit from Ryobi—which is not going to make you the envy of any job site, but offers great value and torque for the money. This set offers a ½-inch drill/driver, an impact driver, a circular saw, and an LED light. There's also another discount kit with a sander, drill/driver, and circular saw.

Home Depot DeWalt Tool BOGO

My editor, Kat Merck, is a DeWalt devotee. But the DeWalt Deals are a bit more specialized this season. There's still a few good BOGO offers, though, especially if you're in the market for a circular saw or angle grinder, or a hammer drill kit to carve holes into masonry.

entries.title: Best Tech Labor Day Sales I’d Shop Myself (2026): Vacuums, Headphones, and More
entries.summary: From cordless vacuums to the best wireless earbuds we’ve tested, some of our favorite tech is on sale for Labor Day this year.
entries.content:
The last long weekend of summer has arrived, and with it, a slew of cart-worthy deals. While summer won't officially end for a few weeks, something about Labor Day feels like the last hurrah, and it makes for the perfect time to snag on-sale gadgets to set you up for a smooth fall and holiday season.

The sales started early this year, but they're still going strong with plenty of our favorite tech gear discounted during the holiday weekend. You can shop everything from high-quality headphones to Dyson vacuums and Apple AirTags. Every item we feature is a tech gadget the WIRED Reviews team has tested and loved, and a top pick from our guides ranging from headphones and speakers to vacuums and chargers.

Updated September 5: I've added new vacuum and smart home deals, and ensured all deals are still live.

WIRED Featured Tech Deals

Labor Day Deals on Tech Gadgets

This is the best Labor Day laptop deal we've found, which takes $700 off the HP OmniBook Ultra 14. It's one of our favorite new laptops to come out this year, sporting an absolutely immaculate design and a brilliant OLED display. We especially like the look of the large haptic trackpad and keycaps of the white version, though it's the black one that's on sale here. Beyond just being easy on eyes, it also performs like a dream, with both strong performance and fantastic battery life. While we liked the device when we reviewed it, it was quite expensive, and we'd been waiting for the price to drop to give a full-throated recommendation. Well, this is it. For $1,200, you're even getting 32 GB of RAM—double what comes on a MacBook Air at this price.

Need an AirTag to track your keys or luggage (or in my case, my son's backpack when we're on a trip)? Apple's line of Bluetooth trackers can add up if you need to buy a lot, but you can get $5 off a single one right now, or $10 off a four-pack.

If you're a Google Pixel user and you need a new case, Dbrand makes one of our favorite cases for Pixel phones—especially if you're in the market for a clear one. Its Pixelsnap-certified magnets are strong, the edges around the camera are slightly raised for extra protection, and it's grippy. There's no plasticky texture, either, which is nice to find on a clear case.

This charging tray from Courant is, simply put, gorgeous. It comes in both leather and linen finishes, and there are two chargers built into it for your phone and your wireless earbuds. The left charger is MagSafe-compatible, while the right side is a Qi charger you can use with either Apple or non-Apple products.

The best MagSafe car mount is usually pretty affordable, but this discount makes it even more attainable. It's well ventilated and sticks supremely to any flat surface. It's compatible with any MagSafe phone (or any magnetic phone case, which yours should be regardless of operating system.)

Labor Day Deals for Your Home

If you're looking to spend as little as possible without getting a crappy vacuum, Bissell makes our favorite affordable vacuums. The PowerClean and PowerClean FurFinder are both excellent, affordable choices that will still get you solid power, cleaning attachments, and a vacuum you can count on. The PowerClean is often on sale, and a good choice unless you want the special FurFinder attachment for pet hair.

Our top robot vacuum has dropped down to the best deal we've seen. It's often on sale for $850 and regularly jumps back up to its full $1,400 price. But right now, you can get it for just $750. If you're in the market and don't want to wait until fall shopping events like Prime Day or Black Friday, this is a safe buy for a great gadget. Built-in AI intelligently cleans tricky messes, and the extendable arm can reach places other vacuums can't. It also empties its own dust bin when cleaning is done, and it can even lift itself out of a situation when it gets stuck (most of the time).

While a ton of Echo speakers were hit with price increases that lead to worse sales than before, the Echo Show 11 has maintained its same price tag and is on sale for Labor Day weekend. I really like the Echo Show 11's sound quality, and the three extra inches of screen felt like a nice improvement over the Echo Show 8 without overcrowding my counter or desk.

My most life-changing smart device is a smart lock. It makes it possible for everyone in my family—even my four year old—to enter the house without worrying about keys or if someone's home. While my son has the code memorized for our current smart lock, a biometric based lock is even easier since it lets your family members add fingerprints and even their face to unlock the door. For privacy reasons, the Lockly lock uses IR cameras, so there's no live camera feed. It's $50 off, bringing it to the lowest price in the last few months.

Usually smart home devices mean you can control and automate commands like turning on music or lights. So while this calendar isn't technically a true smart home device, it just be might one of the smartest devices in my house. And for unlike so many “smart” devices, this one actually make my life (and my husband's!) easier. It's a digital wall calendar, which lets me sync my digital calendar I already use onto the screen so I can access it whenever I want. There's also meal planning, chore tracking, and some have photo screensavers you can use too. The Everblog is my favorite for not having a subscription, so you can access all kinds of features without paying anything extra like you would on the Skylight.

Speaker and Headphone Labor Day Deals

The best Bluetooth speaker is the JBL Flip 7, and it's on sale for a little more than $50 off ahead of Labor Day. Buying a portable Bluetooth speaker means you won't get everything you'd look for in a speaker, but the Flip 7 has a good balance between mobility and sound quality. It also packs better water resistance than past Flip models and a two-hour battery (or four with reduced bass). Not every color is on sale for this low, but most are at least slightly discounted.

This clip-on speaker packs surprisingly chunky sound for its size. The built-in carabiner means you can easily tote it around while you're on the go, and the onboard controls are easy to find and operate. This deal is solidly in the middle of what we tend to see; sometimes it falls a bit more in price, but this discount isn't a bad one.

This speaker fluctuates in price very often, and it has remained a steadfast budget recommendation in our Bluetooth speaker buying guide. We don't see it fall below $30 frequently. The sound will not blow you away. But for the price, it's decent, with great battery life and a very portable water-resistant design.

They're not the newest Sony headphones we love (the XM6), but at this price, it's hard not to want to spring for it. This is the lowest price it tends to fall to, but it was selling for almost $50 more just a few days ago. Don't get me wrong—the XM6 that came out earlier this year are a significant upgrade, but if you want a beautiful-sounding, comfortable, and stylish pair of noise-canceling headphones, the Sony XM5 will still make you very happy. Especially at this price.

Nothing earbuds consistently earn mentions in our buying guides, and the latest iteration is an honorable mention being sold at a very compelling price. The Nothing Ear (3a) are stylish and have solid sound, intuitive controls, and an optional app that's actually useful. Noise cancellation could be better, but for less than $100 these are still a stellar budget pick.
